prompt:
Here are three short samples of my writing. Match my style in what you write.

Sample 1:
making them play lame chicken.... Now all this done by a young lady who remembers eighteen months ago with so much regret that she has lost so much of her high spirits--might argue that her spirits were before tremendous; and yet they were not. That other Sarah was ladylike, I am sure, in her wildest moments, but there is something hurried and boisterous in this one's tricks that reminds me of some one who is making a merit of being jolly under depressing circumstances. No! that is not a nice Sarah now, to my taste.

The commencement of '61 promised much pleasure for the rest of the year, and though Secession was talked about, I do not believe any one anticipated the war that has been desolating our country ever since, with no prospect of terminating for some time to come. True the garrison was taken, but then several pleasant

Sample 2:
for the best for us in the end; that all has come right in spite of us, we will wonder how we could ever have been foolish enough to await each hour in such breathless anxiety. We will ask ourselves if it was really true that nightly, as we lay down to sleep, we did not dare plan for the morning, feeling that we might be homeless and beggars before the dawn. How unreal it will then seem! We will say it was our wild imagination, perhaps. But how bitterly, horribly true it is now!

Four days ago the Yankees left us, to attack Vicksburg, leaving their flag flying in the Garrison without a man to guard it, and with the understanding that the town would be held responsible for it. It was intended for a trap; and it succeeded. For night before last, it was pulled down and torn

And so, if any man should fancy he cared to kiss me, he could do so under the pretext that I had pulled my dress from under his feet! That will justify them! And if we decline their visits, they can insult us under the plea of a prior affront. Oh! Gibbes! George! Jimmy! never did we need your protection as sorely as now. And not to know even whether you are alive! When Charlie joins the army, we will be defenseless, indeed. Come to my bosom, O my discarded carving-knife, laid aside under the impression that these men were gentlemen. We will be close friends once more. Write a note to a friend about a sleepless night. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Dear Annie,

It is past three o'clock, and I am writing to you by a candle-end because I cannot sleep, and because there is no one else awake to be tiresome to. You must forgive the scrawl. My hand is not steady, though whether from the hour or from the cold, I cannot say.

I went to bed at ten, like a sensible creature, and lay there as straight and stiff as a corpse in its coffin, listening. First it was the clock in the hall, which I never notice by day, and which tonight struck every quarter as if it meant to be heard in the next county. Then it was a shutter that banged, and a dog somewhere down the road that barked at nothing, and then a long silence that was worse than either. I counted the cracks in the ceiling. I counted them again and got a different number. That is the sort of state I was in!

Of course, once the lamp was out, every thought I had managed to put away all day came creeping back, and sat down on the foot of my bed like old acquaintances who have not been invited. Had Mother's letter come? Was there any news of the boys? Would the flour last till Christmas? I answered them one by one, very reasonably, and then they all began again, and I had to start over. I wonder that anyone ever sleeps at all, in times like these. And yet Sister Kate, in the next bed, breathes as softly as a child, and has not stirred once. I could almost have pinched her out of pure envy.

I tried reciting poetry, and got no further than the second verse before I lost my place. I tried praying, and I fear my mind wandered there too, which I hope will be forgiven me. At last I got up, put my shawl about me, and went to the window. The moon was nearly down, and the garden looked so quiet and so silvery that I felt quite ashamed of my fretting. Nothing out there was in any hurry or any trouble. The old pear tree simply stood and waited for morning, as if that were the easiest thing in the world.

Perhaps it is. I shall try to learn it of the pear tree.

Now I shall blow out my candle, and creep back to bed, and very likely fall asleep the moment I have sealed this up. That would be just like me. Write soon, and tell me how you slept.

Your wakeful,
Sarah
